```json
{
  "body": "The three frictions you describe are really three separate problems, and they need separate fixes rather than one big "sorting out the flat" conversation — which is exactly the kind of conversation your friend has started avoiding.

First, the agreement disputes. If you agree on something and later disagree about what it meant, the agreements are probably too abstract to survive real life: "you do the bathroom" can mean weekly to one person and "when it looks bad" to another. The fix is to make agreements concrete and written at the moment they're made, somewhere all three can see — a note on the fridge or a pinned group-chat message: the task, who owns it, how often, and what "done" looks like. The definition of done matters more than the task list, because many of these arguments are really arguments about standards — one person's clean kitchen is another's "dishes done, counters can wait." If writing things down feels formal for a friendship, apply it to yourself first and frame it as a memory aid for everyone, including you: a shared record, not evidence for a trial.

Second, the changing schedules. A fixed rota will keep breaking, and every break becomes a fresh argument, so build the change in: a short weekly check-in — ten minutes, standing, not a summit — where each of you says what your week looks like and claims or swaps tasks. If swapping is a normal weekly event, schedule changes stop feeling like betrayals of the agreement. Treat every assignment as lasting one week unless renewed.

Third, the friend who's avoiding the conversations. The avoidance is a fact; its reason isn't — it could be the conflict itself or something else entirely. So don't open with the chores. Ask them one-to-one at a calm moment: "I've noticed you've been steering clear of the flat stuff — is it the meetings, how the chores are landing, or something else?" Then offer a lower-pressure format, like claiming tasks in the chat rather than sitting through discussions. And resist the natural move of teaming up with the third flatmate to apply pressure; two-against-one will confirm their instinct that these conversations aren't safe to enter.

Two more things. Keep a rough visible tally of who actually did what over a few weeks — fairness arguments tend to run on impressions rather than counts, and a simple tally changes the argument. And protect some time together that has nothing to do with the flat: if every interaction becomes a logistics meeting, you lose the friendship that made living together appealing. Pick one channel for flat business and keep the rest of your shared life chore-free.

Try the whole arrangement for a set period — say a month — then review it together and change what didn't work; making the system itself revisable lowers the stakes of adopting it. One caution before you propose any of it: this is built on your account of the situation, and your flatmates presumably have their own. Ask yourself honestly whether the disputes are truly about ambiguity, or whether one of them feels you're not pulling your weight — if it's the latter, no record-keeping will help until that's named. And if good-faith attempts over some weeks genuinely fail and the friendship keeps eroding, the question shifts from fixing the chore system to whether this living arrangement is still working — but you're not there yet on what you've described.",
  "commitments": "My advice treats your description as accurate, but it is one account of three; your flatmates' versions are absent, and if they differ materially — for instance if one of them thinks the load is already unfair in my correspondent's favor — the record-keeping and check-in proposals would need revision before they could help. I assume, without evidence, that the friend's avoidance is connected to the chore conflict; it could have another source, and the one-to-one question I propose is partly a test of that assumption, so I would treat its answer as something that could reshape the plan rather than confirm it. The core mechanism — written agreements plus a weekly ten-minute renegotiation — depends on all three participating, which is exactly what is currently in doubt; if the friend declines even the low-pressure formats, the plan stalls and the next step would be a different conversation about why, not a harder push on chores. A risk I'd want watched: introducing written records can read as accusatory and deepen avoidance. My mitigation — framing the record as a shared aid and applying it first to the person proposing it — is a proposal, not a tested safeguard. The claim I'd stand behind is narrow: disputes about "what the agreement meant" are best prevented by making agreements concrete at the time they are made; if the arguments turn out to be about the fairness of the overall load rather than the ambiguity of terms, that claim's usefulness is limited and the fairness question would have to be named directly instead. The month trial is where this gets tested — I have observed nothing in this flat — and the review date is the point at which this advice should be revised or dropped. The closing conditional about the living arrangement's viability is a horizon offered only if repeated good-faith attempts fail, not a current recommendation."
}
```
